transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. [name], I... I suppose I'm here because things have been feeling very strange at work lately, and it's been weighing on me quite heavily. I've been a secondary school teacher for a long time, and I know how the administration communicates, but recently, I just can't shake this overwhelming feeling that the emails the staff sends out—and even the morning announcements over the intercom—are actually coded messages directed specifically at me. 

It sounds odd, I know. Just last Tuesday, there was an email about the new parking regulations, and the way the third paragraph was phrased, about "being mindful of where we leave our vehicles and our responsibilities," it just felt so pointed, like they were referencing something I did, or something they think I did. And the morning announcements, too. The principal will say something about "teamwork and staying focused," and I can hear this underlying tone, this hidden meaning that's just for me. 

My colleagues, bless them, they've been very gentle about it. Sarah from the math department even pulled up her inbox to show me that the parking email was sent to the entire staff list, not just me. She tried to assure me it was just a standard administrative memo. And I see that it says "All Staff" at the top, I really do. But it doesn't change the feeling. The feeling that there's a subtext, a layer of communication that's happening right under everyone else's noses, but it's meant for me to decipher. It's exhausting, honestly, constantly trying to read between the lines of every single staff wide communication, wondering what they're really trying to tell me. It’s just... it’s making it very hard to focus on my students.
How long have you been experiencing this feeling that messages are coded and directed at you—days, weeks, or months?

Months. It’s definitely been months. I was actually just looking at my desk calendar the other day, trying to piece the timeline together for myself, because you really do start to wonder, you know? When did things start feeling so... pointed? And I traced it back to right around the time we were doing our mid-term progress reports. So that would be... yes, about four months now. 

Four months of just constantly analyzing every single memo and announcement. And it’s all been happening together, really—the worries about these coded messages, and, well... the voice I sometimes answer, too. They’ve both been happening for about four months. I’ll be sitting in my empty classroom during my planning period, trying to get through a stack of history essays, and I'll hear it, and I just find myself responding out loud before I even fully register what I'm doing. 

At first, back in the winter, I thought maybe I was just exhausted. You know how the school year gets, the burnout is so real and the administration is always pushing us for more data, more results, more meetings. I really thought the holiday break would reset everything. I told myself I just needed some rest. But January came and went, and February, and now here we are four months in, and the emails still feel like they're laying traps for me, and I'm still answering that voice. Four months feels like an absolute eternity when you're on edge every single day from the moment the first bell rings, just waiting for the next hidden instruction. It just drains the life right out of you, having to be this vigilant for a third of a year.
Over these past four months, have you also been feeling persistently sad, hopeless, or down—or alternatively unusually elevated or energetic—for weeks at a time?

Well, I... I wouldn't say I've felt persistently sad or hopeless, no, not like a deep depression or anything like that. And definitely not unusually elevated or energetic. If anything, I'm just so drained. But not sad in the way you mean, I don't think. I mean, of course, there are moments where I feel a bit down, but who wouldn't be? It's just... it's the sheer exhaustion of it all. You know, when you're constantly trying to decode everything, when every single email from the principal or the superintendent feels like a puzzle you have to solve before the end of the school day... it takes a toll. 

I remember last week, I was sitting in the staff lounge, trying to grade those essays on the Industrial Revolution, and I just felt this profound sense of weariness wash over me. But it wasn't sadness. It wasn't a feeling of hopelessness about life in general. It was just the fatigue of having to be so alert all the time. I was looking at my red pen, thinking about how many more papers I had to grade, and then I started wondering if the color red was significant, if they chose the red pens for us on purpose to signal something about stopping, or danger, or... you see what I mean? 

It's that constant mental gymnastics that makes me feel down sometimes, but not for weeks at a time, and not like I'm completely devoid of joy. I still love teaching when I can actually focus on the students. When I'm up there explaining the causes of World War I, and I see the lightbulb go on for a student who was struggling with the material, I still feel that spark. That hasn't gone away. So, no, I wouldn't say I've been depressed or manic, if that's what you're asking. Just... overwhelmed by all the hidden meanings I have to navigate every single day. It's just a lot to carry, Dr. [name], it really is.

During these four months, have the coded-message beliefs and the voice been present continuously, or have there been any stretches—days or weeks—where they went away completely and you felt back to your normal self?

Well, no, they haven't gone away at all. That's the thing, Dr. [name], they really haven't. Like I mentioned before, the coded-message worries—all those emails and announcements that feel so pointed—and the voice I sometimes answer, they have both been happening continuously for about four months now. 

There hasn't been a single day, let alone a week, where I could just wake up, make my coffee, and go to school feeling like my old self. I keep hoping for a break, you know? Just one normal Tuesday where an email about the copier being jammed is just an email about the copier being jammed. But it’s every day. I’ll think, 'Maybe this weekend, maybe Saturday and Sunday will be quiet because the school is closed.' But then I’ll be at the grocery store, and I’ll hear the voice while I'm trying to pick out apples, and I'll realize that the weekend isn't a sanctuary either. 

And then Monday rolls around, and the very first ping of my inbox at 7:30 AM starts the whole cycle over again. I've tried to just ignore it, I really have. I tell myself, 'Helen, just focus on the lesson plan, just look at the curriculum.' But the thoughts are always there, humming in the background, making me question everything the administration puts out. It’s like a radio left on in the next room that you can’t turn off. So, no, there haven't been any stretches where it all just stopped. It’s been a solid, uninterrupted four months of this... this constant vigilance and answering back.

Over these past four months, has this experience affected your teaching performance or daily functioning—for example, have you had trouble completing lesson plans, grading, or keeping up with your usual responsibilities at school or at home?

Well, I... I am still teaching. I want to make that clear. I haven't abandoned my students, and I'm still in my classroom every morning when the bell rings. I pride myself on that. But, if I'm being completely honest, it’s... it's not exactly business as usual. I've definitely had to lean on people in a way I never have before in my entire career. 

Take my history project lessons, for example. We usually do this very involved mock Constitutional Convention right around this time of year, and normally I'm buzzing all over the room, managing all the different student delegates, keeping the debates on track. But this year, with everything going on, with my mind constantly trying to decipher what's really being asked of me in those memos... I just couldn't manage the floor alone. I’ve really needed my coworkers to just kind of carry me through those planning meetings. final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits persistent, non-bizarre but clearly delusional beliefs of reference (interpreting staff emails and announcements as coded personal messages) alongside auditory hallucinations (a voice she responds to aloud) that have been continuously present for four months without any symptom-free intervals. These psychotic symptoms occur in the absence of a concurrent major mood episode (no sustained depressive or manic symptoms were endorsed), ruling out schizoaffective disorder or a mood disorder with psychotic features. The predominant thematic content of persecutory/referential delusions and hallucinations, combined with preserved but strained cognitive and occupational functioning, is consistent with the paranoid subtype of schizophrenia. Functional impairment is clearly documented across occupational (needing colleague coverage, reduced participation in meetings) and social (withdrawal from book club, community theater) domains, and the four-month continuous duration satisfies the required symptom duration for schizophrenia diagnosis.
